To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the problem of catastrophic forgetting in sequence-to-sequence tasks is more complex than in image classification tasks, and that it can be mitigated with a simple memory-augmented architecture; (2) the performance degradation of a sequence-to-sequence model when dealing with a changing task distribution can be measured in terms of accuracy, but also in terms of the amount of data that needs to be processed in order to achieve the desired performance, which is an important metric for real-world applications.
(1) catastrophic forgetting and task interferences are a problem in sequential data processing; and (2) GIM is an effective architecture for addressing these problems in RNNs.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we provide a novel benchmark for evaluating the continual learning capabilities of recurrent neural networks, and we introduce a general architecture that is able to achieve state-of-the-art results in this task.

, in order to learn from a sequence of tasks, recurrent models must be endowed with a mechanism for controlling the flow of information from previous tasks to current ones, and that the Gated Incremental memory is such a mechanism.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, while catastrophic forgetting is not a problem for recurrent models, task interference is a major issue that can be addressed by leveraging incremental memory mechanisms.
the problem of catastrophic forgetting is not only relevant for sequence processing but can also be mitigated through the introduction of simple and efficient incremental memory architectures.

the problem of catastrophic forgetting is not as critical as it has been claimed to be for recurrent models, and that the proposed architecture can be successfully applied to a wide range of sequential data processing tasks.
